description: Building things that make a positive impact!
summary:
Jezero Crater Expedition is an interactive 3D browser-based astronaut training simulation designed for kids ages 7 to 12. Playable instantly in the browser with no downloads required, it guides young cadets from pre-flight boarding at Kennedy Space Center to a five-Sol survival mission at Jezero Crater, Mars, and a parachute return to Earth.

To address the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, every in-game hazard and outpost task is grounded in six official NASA and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) datasets: Perseverance MEDA weather and rover photos, DONKI space weather, RadLab radiation dosimetry, OSDR space biology studies, Mars Trek terrain data, and the CSA Space Food Production toolkit. Players manage a strict 110-Watt zero-sum power budget across three systems: Mobility, Suit Heaters, and Radiation Shields. Because boosting heaters during a freezing Martian night drains power from shields and movement, learners experience real aerospace trade-offs firsthand.

By pairing plain-language Earth comparisons with non-punitive coaching from a voiced 3D Senior Astronaut mentor, our project makes authentic NASA science accessible, engaging, and unforgettable for the next generation of explorers.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

Jezero Crater Expedition is an interactive 3D browser-based astronaut training simulator that takes children ages 7 to 12 (and curious adults) through a complete human Mars mission. The experience unfolds across three connected phases:

  • Phase 1 (Pre-Flight and Launch at Kennedy Space Center): Players meet Senior Astronaut Commander Sunita Williams at Launch Complex 39B, walk across the pad, ride the high-speed tower elevator, cross the swinging Crew Access Arm into the sterile White Room, and launch toward Mars.
  • Phase 2 (Five-Sol Survival at Jezero Crater, Mars): Stepping down the lander stairs at Octavia E. Butler Landing, cadets must survive five Martian days (Sols) of real weather while managing a strict 110-Watt nuclear battery across four interactive stations.
  • Phase 3 (Mars Ascent and Earth Return): After completing all five Sols and collecting golden rock sample tubes, players board the Mars Ascent Vehicle, blast into deep space, survive atmospheric re-entry, and land under three NASA parachutes at Kennedy Space Center.

The Core Engineering Mechanic: A 110-Watt Zero-Sum Trade-Off

Real spaceflight requires constant engineering trade-offs under limited resources. Players split 110 Watts of shared power between three competing suit and base systems:

  1. Mobility Thrusters [1]: Controls walking speed against high Martian winds and 0.38g jump calibration.
  2. Suit and Greenhouse Heaters [2]: Protects astronaut body warmth and hydroponic crop roots during freezing -84.6°C Martian nights.
  3. Radiation Shield and Radar [3]: Defends the outpost against solar energetic particle storms and thick dust plumes.

Because total power cannot exceed 100%, there is no safe passive setting. Boosting heaters to survive a deep freeze automatically reduces power to shields and mobility, teaching kids to actively adapt their strategy to live environmental data.

How Real NASA and CSA Data Drive the Simulation

Every hazard, task, and discovery is mathematically driven by six official NASA and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) resources. In full compliance with challenge guidelines, our interface clearly distinguishes between our embedded Curated Real NASA and CSA Dataset and our Live NASA API Sync mode:

  • NASA Open APIs and Mars 2020 MEDA: Real Perseverance temperature, pressure, wind speed, and dust optical depth (Tau) directly control 3D atmospheric fog density, solar panel wattage drops, and suit heater drain rates, alongside real Mastcam-Z surface photos.
  • NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database): Real solar flare and coronal mass ejection records trigger ultraviolet Martian auroras on Sol 4 and require players to align the outpost radar dish.
  • NASA OSDR RadLab (Radiation Dosimetry): Real absorbed radiation dose rates (comparing the 210 µGy/day Mars baseline and 4,850 µGy/day solar storm spikes against ISS dosimetry) govern shield depletion.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR): Scanning rock samples at the Perseverance Rover unlocks findings from real spaceflight biology studies (OSD-104, OSD-379, OSD-321, and OSD-482) covering bone density, muscle mass in 0.38g gravity, and immune response.
  • NASA Mars Trek: Anchors the 3D outpost terrain and navigation compass at real Jezero Crater coordinates (18.4447°N, 77.4508°E at -2,540m elevation).
  • Canadian Space Agency (CSA) Space Food Production Toolkit: Grounds the Hydroponics Dome in real lunar and remote greenhouse methods, where harvesting dwarf tomatoes, red leaf lettuce, and radishes replenishes astronaut oxygen (0.84 kg O2/day).

Creativity and Factors Our Team Considered

  • Non-Punitive Mentor Coaching: Instead of frustrating "Game Over" screens, when warmth or shielding runs low, a Mission Safety Pause brings 3D Commander Sunita Williams beside the player to explain the exact NASA weather reading and coach them on rebalancing their battery to resume immediately.
  • Plain Language Without Prior Knowledge: Pressing [T] opens the Kid's Mars Guide, which translates complex metrics into relatable everyday comparisons (such as comparing a -84°C Martian night to a -18°C kitchen freezer).
  • Authentic Martian Physics and Acoustics: Jumping in 0.38g gravity features a biomechanical knee crouch and locked mid-air ballistic momentum. Our custom Web Audio synthesizer recreates the low-pitched 80 to 240 Hz Martian wind profile recorded by Perseverance's microphone.
  • Dynamic Replayability: A randomized space weather seed varies telemetry and emergencies across playthroughs so students can test new resource strategies every time.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Zero Barrier to Entry: The simulation runs directly in any modern desktop or laptop browser with no downloads, installations, or user accounts required.
  • Empowering Global STEM Classrooms: By turning abstract NASA spreadsheets into tangible 3D cause-and-effect choices, Jezero Crater Expedition equips teachers, museums, and young learners worldwide to think like real mission planners.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used

  • Languages and Core Framework: TypeScript, JavaScript (ES2022), HTML5, CSS3, React 18, and Vite.
  • 3D Graphics and Physics Engine: Three.js, React Three Fiber (@react-three/fiber), React Three Drei (@react-three/drei), and a custom real-time CPU/GPU vertex skeletal skinning deformer built for NASA's official 3D spacesuit and Perseverance Rover (.glb) models.
  • State, Styling, and Audio: Zustand for 60 FPS transient state management, Tailwind CSS v4 for frosted-glass UI components, Web Audio API for procedural rocket and Martian wind synthesis, and Web Speech API for dual-character voice synthesis (mature female voice for the Commander and child voice for the Junior Cadet).
  • AI-Assisted Development Workflow: Kimi CLI for rapid TypeScript and Three.js component scaffolding and code refactoring, and Google Gemini for aerospace architecture planning, NASA/CSA dataset cross-referencing, and technical documentation structuring. All scientific constants, mission rules, and 3D interactions were manually directed, tested, and verified against official NASA and CSA sources.
  • Deployment and Data Pipeline: Hosted on Vercel with serverless environment configuration connected to NASA Open APIs (api.nasa.gov) and the NASA OSDR Search API.
